## Introduction

## Exploratory data analysis

The provided dataset consists of a four dimensional array comprised of 25 000 handwritten digits of 28 by 28 pixels and associated metadata. The five digits from 0 to 4 were each replicated 50 times by 20 different individuals during each of five independent sessions. The array contained no missing values, indicating all images were complete. Pixel values ranged from zero, indicating a blank background, to 255, representing a pixel completely covered in ink. 

Variation arose between individuals in several different ways (@fig-inter-ind_var). The size of digits written by different people varied and this was particularly pronounced in the digit zero. For example, individuals 3 and 12 had much smaller zeros than individuals 1, 10, and 16 (@fig-inter-ind_var). The angle of lines as well as the curve of the lines within the digits varied. The vertical line in digit one which was straight and vertical for individual 1, more curved for individual 3 and straight yet more diagonal for individual 10. The diagonal and vertical lines in digit four varied in angle and curvature across individuals, and the zeros tilted in different directions for individuals 10 and 12 compared to 1,3, and 16 (@fig-inter-ind_var). 

While inter-individual variation was more pronounced, there was still variation within individuals both across sessions (@fig-within-ind-var) and within a given session (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). The replicates of a digit for a given individual tended to be similar sized. Variation once again arose in the angle and curvature of certain lines such as the top right hand corner of the zeros which differed slightly and the angle of the horizontal line at the bottom of the digit two (@fig-within-ind-var). Intra-individual variation was more recognisable within an individual across different sessions than within an individual in the same session. For person 16, the line at the bottom of digit two was more a more similar angle across replicates in the same session than across different sessions. Across replicates from the same individual and the same session variability arose more in the density of the pixels which can be seen when looking at the bottom horizontal line of the digit one (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). 

There are some clearly visible limitations when using simulated data for handwritten digits. The first is the presence of unusually straight lines and sharp angles in digits where these are unlikely to occur. An example of this is in the top right corner of the digit zero for person 10 (@fig-inter-ind_var). The second is that in some digits the continuity of the line is interrupted, for example the gaps in the digit 2 in sessions 3,4 and 5 for person 16 (@fig-within-ind-var) and all the selected samples for digit two in session 1 (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). Further, the simulated handwritten data fails to mimic changes in the thickness of the font which is likely to occur in real world data where different people use variable pressure when writing. There is no variation in the style of digits. For example, the digit one can also be written as a single vertical line. In some cases, the simulation also does not look accurate, such as for person threes digit 1 which looks much more similar to a 2 and is unlikely to be written like this in real life.

## Writer identification with a CNN

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# After changing any of the training code, delete the file and render again.
cnn_results_file <- "results/cnn_split.rds"
cnn_retrain <- !file.exists(cnn_results_file)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Split by session: sessions 1-3 train, session 4 validation, session 5 test
train_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session <= 3)
val_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session == 4)
test_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session == 5)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Scale pixel values to 0,1
x <- handwriting$images / 255
x_train <- x[train_id,,,,drop = FALSE]
x_val <- x[val_id,,,,drop = FALSE]
x_test <- x[test_id,,,,drop = FALSE]

y <- to_categorical(handwriting$metadata$person_id - 1, 20)
y_train <- y[train_id,]
y_val <- y[val_id,]
y_test <- y[test_id,]
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set_random_seed(67)

input <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))

# from lecture slides
output <- input %>%
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3,3)) %>%
  layer_activation('relu') %>%
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.20) %>%
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3,3), activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2)) %>%
  layer_flatten() %>%
  layer_dense(units = 20, activation = 'softmax')

model <- keras_model(inputs = input, outputs = output)
cnn_summary <- capture.output(print(model))

model %>% compile(
  loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.01),
  metrics = c('accuracy'),
)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Stop when accuracy on the validation session has not improved for 10 epochs,
# and go back to the weights from the best epoch
history <- model %>% fit(
  x_train, y_train,
  epochs = 100, batch_size = 8192,
  validation_data = list(x_val, y_val), shuffle = TRUE,
  verbose = 0,
  callbacks = list(
    callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_accuracy", patience = 10,
                            restore_best_weights = TRUE)
  )
)

# Predictions for the validation and test sessions (op_argmax counts from 1, so this is the person_id)
y_val_hat <- model %>% predict(x_val, verbose = 0) %>% op_argmax(axis = 2) %>% as.numeric()
y_test_hat <- model %>% predict(x_test, verbose = 0) %>% op_argmax(axis = 2) %>% as.numeric()

# Save everything the rest of this section needs
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(list(summary = cnn_summary,
             history = tibble(epoch = seq_along(history$metrics$accuracy),
                              train = history$metrics$accuracy,
                              validation = history$metrics$val_accuracy),
             predictions = bind_rows(
               as_tibble(handwriting$metadata[val_id,]) %>% mutate(set = "validation", predicted = y_val_hat),
               as_tibble(handwriting$metadata[test_id,]) %>% mutate(set = "test", predicted = y_test_hat))),
        cnn_results_file)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

## Writer verification with a Siamese network


<!-- Task 3: contrastive or triplet loss; how training examples are constructed; matching performance. -->

A Siamese network was trained on the handwriting images to evaluate how accurately it could capture whether two digits were written by the same writer. 
To do so, we had to control for the digit identity by constructing pairs using the same digit. Therefore, a positive pair for this network consists of the same digit done by the same writer (but different images), and a negative pair is the same digit but a different writer. Examples of pairs from the training and validation datasets is shown in @fig-pairs.

We conducted balanced sampling for the pairs, so that half of the pairs came from the same person and half different (check; rephrase).

Contrastive loss was used - (do I need a justification?) - which introduces another hyperparameter for model tuning: the margin, $m$. The formula is:
$$
L = yD^2 + (1-y)\max(0,m-D)^2
$$
where $y = 1$ for a positive pair (same writer, same digit) and $D$ is the Euclidean distance between the embeddings. $m$ sets the distance at which embeddings for similar pairs results in zero loss (where the distance reaches the margin) versus embeddings for dissimilar pairs resulting in a large loss, thereby optimising the network to minimise differences between image pairs from the same writer and maximising differences between image pairs from different writers @ELARABY20221837. The margin for this initial Siamese network was set as 1 [following the notes], but was optimised in (ref section 5).

The training/validation/test data splitting was done on writer-level to ensure that the network learns the writing style, or writer identity, and so that the generalisability of the model can be tested (accurately/with minimal leakage) with writers it hasn't seen in training or validation. However, since there are only 20 writers, a 60/20/20 split leaves only 4 writers for validation and testing independently, which is a significant limitation and is expanded in (ref section 4).

The encoder architecture was set as a simple CNN with two convolutional layers, max pooling and global pooling...
[because the input images are low-resolution and contain (easily learnable) features like curves and strokes] 

The Siamese model outputs distances between the two embeddings for each digit pair, which is then turned into a classification of "same" or "different" writer using a threshold determined by the validation pairs [also a limitation with the few writers & the split we have]. We compared the balanced accuracy for actual same and different digit pairs at different thresholds, and chose the threshold with the maximised balanced accuracy. 

The generalisability of our model was evaluated by predicting on unseen writers' digit image-pairs. The results are shown in @tab-confusionmat and @tab-testresults. @fig-test-results shows the test batch's predicted and true results



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# need pairs of image indices to compare
# use person_id to decide if positive / negative pair

make_pairs <- function(ids, # indices of images it can use
                       n, # how many pairs to create
                       metadata){ # metadata -> writer ID + digit ID for each image
  
  # a: choose the first image in every pair - randomly selects n IDs
  a <- sample(ids, n, replace = TRUE) # w/replacement = can make as many pairs as we want
  
  # b: create the second image in every pair
  b <- vapply(a, function(i){
    
    # randomly decide if pair is from same writer or not
    same <- runif(1) < 0.5 
    
    # finds pool of images with the same digit
    pool <- ids[metadata$digit[ids] == metadata$digit[i]]
    
    if(same){ # if the same writer, pool must be same writer + same digit (pos pair)
      
      # 'from all images of digit i, keep only the ones written by the same writer'
      # CHANGE TO Y_PERSON OR NOT?
      pool <- pool[metadata$person_id[pool] == metadata$person_id[i]]# who wrote image i
      
    } else { # if not the same writer, pool must be diff writer + same digit (neg pair)
      
      pool <- pool[metadata$person_id[pool] != metadata$person_id[i]]
      
    }
    sample(setdiff(pool, i), 1) # doesn't allow pairing with itself
    
  }, integer(1)) # each iteration must return 1 integer
  
  cbind(a,b)
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
make_batch <- function(p, # pairs created by make_pairs()
                       images = x, # actual images
                       class_labels = y_person) { # class assoc with images
  
  y <- matrix(as.integer( # true = 1, false = 0
    class_labels[p[, 1]] # labels of first col of p-i matrix
                         == class_labels[p[, 2]]), # label of second col
              ncol = 1) # matrix of 1 col for formatting for neural network
  
  # return the actual images + the target
  list(
    left = images[p[, 1], , , , drop = FALSE], # left side of Siamese
    right = images[p[, 2], , , , drop = FALSE], # right side of Siamese
    y = y
  )
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
a <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
b <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))

# encoders produce the embeddings for a & b
# distance calculates the Euclidean distance between their embeddings 
distance <- list(encoder(a), encoder(b)) |>
  layer_lambda(f = function(z) {
    op_sqrt(op_sum(op_square(z[[1]] - z[[2]]), 
                   axis = 2, # sum over embedding dimension
                   keepdims = TRUE) + 
              1e-7) # makes sure it's not 0
  })

# distance = model output
model <- keras_model(list(a, b), distance)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
contrastive_loss <- function(y, d) {
  op_mean( # finds avg loss across all pairs in a batch
    y * op_square(d) + # squares each pair's distance - for same-writer pairs, penalises a large distance
            (1 - y) * op_square(op_maximum(1 - d, 0))) # for diff writer pairs, penalises only if distance is < 1: if dist >=1, penalty is 0
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Hyper-params:
# the number of filters in both convolution layers, the dropout rate and the learning rate
build_model <- function(filters, dropout, learning_rate) {
  input <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))

  output <- input %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = filters, kernel_size = c(3,3)) %>%
    layer_activation('relu') %>%
    layer_dropout(rate = dropout) %>%
    layer_conv_2d(filters = filters, kernel_size = c(3,3), activation = "relu") %>%
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = c(2, 2)) %>%
    layer_flatten() %>%
    layer_dense(units = 20, activation = 'softmax')

  model <- keras_model(inputs = input, outputs = output)

  model %>% compile(
    loss = 'categorical_crossentropy',
    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = learning_rate),
    metrics = c('accuracy'),
  )

  model
}

# 4-fold cross-validation by session over sessions 1-4 for every row of a grid.
# No early stopping: every combination trains for the same number of epochs and the
# validation accuracy is recorded after each epoch (batch size is fixed at 128).
cv_grid <- function(grid, epochs) {
  grid_history <- list()

  for (i in 1:nrow(grid)) {
    for (fold in 1:4) {
      train_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session <= 4 & handwriting$metadata$session != fold)
      val_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session == fold)

      set_random_seed(67)
      model <- build_model(grid$filters[i], grid$dropout[i], grid$learning_rate[i])

      history <- model %>% fit(
        x[train_id,,,,drop = FALSE], y[train_id,],
        epochs = epochs, batch_size = 128,
        validation_data = list(x[val_id,,,,drop = FALSE], y[val_id,]), shuffle = TRUE,
        verbose = 0
      )

      grid_history[[paste(i, fold)]] <- tibble(
        learning_rate = grid$learning_rate[i], dropout = grid$dropout[i], filters = grid$filters[i],
        fold = fold, epoch = 1:epochs,
        train = history$metrics$accuracy,
        validation = history$metrics$val_accuracy)
    }
  }

  bind_rows(grid_history)
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# For every combination: the cross-validated accuracy (mean over the four folds) at each epoch,
# the best epoch, and the earliest epoch within one standard error of the best (as in lambda.1se)
summarise_grid <- function(grid_history) {
  grid_history %>%
    group_by(learning_rate, dropout, filters, epoch) %>%
    summarise(cv_accuracy = mean(validation), cv_se = sd(validation) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop_last") %>%
    mutate(best_epoch = epoch[which.max(cv_accuracy)],
           best_accuracy = max(cv_accuracy),
           best_se = cv_se[which.max(cv_accuracy)]) %>%
    filter(cv_accuracy >= best_accuracy - best_se) %>%
    slice_min(epoch, n = 1) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(learning_rate, dropout, filters, best_epoch, best_accuracy, best_se,
           epoch_1se = epoch, accuracy_1se = cv_accuracy) %>%
    arrange(desc(best_accuracy))
}

# Learning rate on the x axis, one line per dropout rate, one panel per number of filters
plot_grid <- function(grid_summary) {
  ggplot(grid_summary, aes(x = learning_rate, y = best_accuracy, colour = factor(dropout))) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = unique(grid_summary$learning_rate)) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
    facet_wrap(~ filters, labeller = labeller(filters = function(f) paste("Filters:", f))) +
    labs(x = "Learning rate", y = "Accuracy (cross-validation)", colour = "Dropout rate") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}

# A grid summary as a formatted table, with accuracies as percentages
table_grid <- function(grid_summary) {
  grid_summary %>%
    mutate(learning_rate = format(learning_rate, scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE),
           across(c(best_accuracy, best_se, accuracy_1se), ~ 100 * .x)) %>%
    select(learning_rate, dropout, filters, best_accuracy, best_se, best_epoch, epoch_1se, accuracy_1se) %>%
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Learning rate", "Dropout rate", "Filters", "Best CV accuracy (%)", "Standard error (%)",
                               "Best epoch", "One-SE epoch", "CV accuracy at one-SE epoch (%)"),
                 digits = 1, align = "r")
}
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Train the selected combination on sessions 1-4, then predict the test session once
train_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session <= 4)
test_id <- which(handwriting$metadata$session == 5)

set_random_seed(67)
model <- build_model(cnn_hpo_selected$filters, cnn_hpo_selected$dropout, cnn_hpo_selected$learning_rate)

model %>% fit(
  x[train_id,,,,drop = FALSE], y[train_id,],
  epochs = cnn_hpo_selected$epoch_1se, batch_size = 128,
  shuffle = TRUE, verbose = 0
)

y_test_hat <- model %>% predict(x[test_id,,,,drop = FALSE], verbose = 0) %>% op_argmax(axis = 2) %>% as.numeric()

saveRDS(as_tibble(handwriting$metadata[test_id,]) %>% mutate(predicted = y_test_hat), cnn_hpo_test_file)
```
